messages.subject: COMPARING DENSITY ESTMATES
messages.body_plain:
Dear All:

I am a field biologist doing line transect surveys of mammals and birds
in forests of India since 1986. For analysis I now use program DISTANCE.
When comparing density estimates between two sites, or two periods at
the same site, or among several different sites, I have been using the
frame work of hypothesis testing (T, Z tests, and ANOVA).

I recently came across Burnham and Andersons (1998) excellent book on
model selection using information theoretic approaches which seems to
suggest that classical hypothesis testing is not the best way to compare
models. Soon after, I came across some ideas in philosophy of science
such as that of David Stove (1998)-who entirely disagrees with the
concept of 'science' as defined by Popper, Lakatos, Kunh and Feyerabend:
and the ideas of Giere (1999) who essentially argues that scientists
constantly strive to build better and better models of true nature...and
they do so by selecting among competing models of true nature which they
try to build.  These ideas seem to tie in with Burnham and Andersons
idea that hypothesis testing in the classical Popperian tradition may
not be best way to select a model (in our case of the detection curve)..

My question is: there a better way than the classical hypothesis testing
to compare several or even two estimates densities (assuming they are
all derived using the best model selected based on say AIC..), without
relying on the hypothesis testing frame-work?  If so how can one
implement such an approach using program DISTANCE or in some other
manner? I apologize in advance if these are dumb questions, I am neither
a statistician nor a philosopher of science..but would like to learn
more from scholars in both these fields..Thanks,

ULLAS KARANTH

CITATIONS:

KP Burnham and DR Anderson (1998): Model Selection and Inference.
Springer Verlag, NY

RN Giere (1999): Science Without Laws. University of Chicago Press.

DC Stove (1998: Anything goes: Origins of the cult of scientific
irrationalism. Macleay Press, Paddington, Australia (originally
published in 1982 as Popper and after: Four modern irrationalists,
Pergamon Press, Oxford).

DR. K. ULLAS KARANTH
WCS-INDIA PROGRAM
403, SEEBO APARTMENTS
26-2, AGA ABBAS ALI ROAD
BANGALORE - 560 042
INDIA

EMAIL: <ukar...@vsnl.com>

messages.body_plain:

Date: Thu, 2 Sep 1999 17:51:18 +0100 (BST)
From: st...@mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk
To: distance...@mailbase.ac.uk

My own view is that all approaches have their pros and cons.  I agree with
the criticisms of hypothesis testing, and conceptually prefer AIC, but if
it would lead you to radically different conclusions from appropriately
applied hypothesis tests, I would be surprised.

If you have two sets of perpendicular distances, and you want to know
whether to pool them or to fit separate detection functions, an easy
solution is to do both.  Then sum the AICs for the two separate fits, and
compare the sum with the AIC from fitting the pooled data.  Choose the
option that gives the smaller AIC.

BUT as in all cookbook recipes, use with caution and commonsense.  Look at
histograms of the data, at goodness-of-fit (despite all its shortcomings),
at the assumptions that might be violated, and try to get a good
understanding of your data.  You may well choose to go with an option
that doesn't give the smallest AIC - though it will probably be not far
off.  (eg the negative exponential may well give the smallest AIC, but we
would never advocate that it be used, because we know its shape close to
zero distance - critical for estimating density - does not match our
physical understanding of the detection process.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: JOB: 3 posts in statistical ecology, St Andrews, Scotland
messages.body_plain:
_______________________________________________________

    U N I V E R S I T Y   O F   S T   A N D R E W S
_______________________________________________________

   School of Mathematical and Computational Sciences

              Centre for Research into
        Ecological and Environmental Modelling
_______________________________________________________

            3 Posts in Statistical Ecology
_______________________________________________________

As part of a major initiative to set up a new centre,
we are seeking to appoint three new staff.

Post 1:  Research Fellow 1A / Research Fellow 2 -
                                     Ref: KC041/AMC1/99

A post for an applied statistician, initially for at
least 1.5 years, exists in the Research Unit for
Wildlife Population Assessment (RUWPA;  see
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk).  You will spend up to
half your time working on projects within the Sea Mammal
Research Unit (SMRU;  see http://smub.st-and.ac.uk/).
Depending on experience and expertise, you will also
work on projects in one or more of the following areas:
development of sightings survey methodology;  spatial
and spatio-temporal modelling of species abundance;
generalized additive models (GAMs);  state-space
modelling;  assessment of cetacean abundance;  surveys
of red, roe and sika deer in Scotland;  fisheries stock
assessments.

You should have a good honours degree in statistics, or
a good honours degree in biology or mathematics with a
strong statistical background, and several years'
experience as an applied statistician. A PhD in a
relevant topic would be a strong advantage, as would
extensive experience with any of the following:  GAMs;
MCMC methods;  state-space models;  wildlife assessment
methods;  S-Plus.  You should be able to communicate
well and enthusiastically with biologists, and should
have consultancy experience.
________________________________________________________

Post 2:  Research Fellow 1A - Ref: KC042/AMC1/99

A post, initially for one year, is available in RUWPA,
also closely linked with SMRU.  You will develop a
simulation model of harbour porpoise dynamics in the
North Sea and adjacent waters.  Following a general
methodology devised by the International Whaling
Commission, the simulation model will evaluate the
consequences of management actions by explicitly
addressing the key area of uncertainty concerning
porpoise population structure and dynamics, based on
the limited available information.

You should have a PhD and experience in mathematical
modelling of biological populations, or other relevant
experience.  You will be hard-working, self-motivated
and innovative.  Ideally, you would have had exposure to
modelling work conducted by the International Whaling
Commission.
________________________________________________________

Post 3:  Research Fellow 1A - Ref: KC154/AMC1/99

This position is available on combining population
dynamic modelling and statistical modelling for
ecological impact assessment.  The idea is to integrate
population dynamic models within a statistical modelling
framework, in order to improve ecological predictions for
impact assessment.  The work will build on existing
methodology developed at St. Andrews for fitting and
inference using population dynamic models, the structure
of which may include non-parametric smooth terms.  The
project provides much scope for innovative work in
population dynamics and methodological statistics.  The
post is funded by Zeneca Agrochemicals (as part of its
strategic research program) and will involve collaboration
with Dr Tim Kedwards and colleagues in Zeneca's ecological
risk assessment section based at Jealott's Hill in
Berkshire.   You will work at St Andrews with Dr Simon
Wood at the Mathematical Institute.  You should have a PhD
or expect to obtain one shortly, although candidates
without a PhD may be considered if they have suitable
experience.  The position is available for 2 years in the
first instance.

Informal inquiries should be directed to Steve Buckland:
st...@st-and.ac.uk.

Salary will be at the appropriate point on the RA1A scale
for research staff ie 16,286 - 24,479 pounds per annum or in
the case of post 1, for an exceptional candidate, Scale 2
ie 22,579- 30,065 pounds per annum. (1 UK pound = US$1.62.)

Closing Date for Posts 1 and 2:  7 October 1999
Closing Date for Post 3:  27 September 1999

Application forms and further particulars from Personnel
Services, University of St Andrews, College Gate, North
Street, St Andrews, Fife KY16 9AJ (tel: +44-(0)1334-462571,
fax +44-(0)1334-462570 or e-mail Job...@st-andrews.ac.uk).
We regret applications cannot be made by e-mail.

The University operates Equal Opportunities and No Smoking
Policies.

messages.subject: Density Equation Confirmation
messages.body_plain:
Distance Users,

I would like to comfirm that I am using the correct density equation
within a paper I am currently working on.

Keeping in mind:

 I was measuring the density of clustered populations
 I was only recording data on one side of the transect line
 I used a uniform key model with a simple  polynomial adjustment

therefore D=n*s/Lu

d=density
n= number of groups detected
s= mean size of clusters
L= totallength of transects
u= effective width strip

I would appreciate any comments.  Thank you.

Pamela

messages.subject: Re: Density Equation Confirmation
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 18 Sep 1999 17:48:13 -0400 (EDT), Pamela McRae wrote:

> >I would like to comfirm that I am using the correct density equation
> >within a paper I am currently working on.

Yes, your equation is correct.

> >Keeping in mind:
> >
> > I was measuring the density of clustered populations
> > I was only recording data on one side of the transect line
> > I used a uniform key model with a simple  polynomial adjustment

This last bit of information was not necessary to answer the question - it
doesn't matter what key or adjustment you used - the formula is the same.

> >therefore D=n*s/Lu
> >
> >d=density
> >n= number of groups detected
> >s= mean size of clusters

By using mean cluster size you assume you don't have size bias (Distance
Sampling book, p77-87).

> >L= totallength of transects
> >u= effective width strip

Although we usually call mu (u) the effective strip width, it is actually the
effective strip half-width which is why your equation is correct.

> >I would appreciate any comments.  Thank you.

My comment is that I think this question was a bit easy for sending to the
list - you could have answered it by looking in the Distance Sampling book,
which is available for free online.  Perhaps next time you could consult
someone close to hand (if possible - e.g., Mark Ridgeway in your case) before
broadcasting your request to about 500 people on the list.  However, this is
just my opinion, and I'm probabily biased as I work with this stuff every
day!

All the best,

 - Len Thomas
